subject: humanities
passage: The Bible that Johannes Gutenberg printed in Mainz in the 1450s is often treated as the moment when mechanical reproduction replaced the handmade book. Yet a buyer who acquired one received something unfinished. The printed pages left blank spaces where large initial letters belonged, and headings and chapter markers were generally added in red ink by hand. Purchasers then hired local artists to supply decoration in whatever style and quantity they could afford, so that the surviving copies differ noticeably from one another. In its own time, the most famous printed book in Europe was, in a real sense, still partly a manuscript.
stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To explain why surviving copies of the Gutenberg Bible are now so rare and so valuable
choices.B: To complicate a common view of an early printed book by showing the handwork it required
choices.C: To argue that Gutenberg's printing press was far less important than historians have claimed
choices.D: To describe the decorative styles that artists in fifteenth-century Mainz preferred

explanation.why: The text begins with a common view, that Gutenberg's Bible marks the replacement of the handmade book, and then says "Yet" each copy was "unfinished," needing handwritten headings and hand-painted decoration. The last sentence concludes that the book was "still partly a manuscript." The text complicates the common view.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the copies differ from one another but says nothing about their rarity or value.
explanation.B: Correct. The text sets up the view that printing replaced handmade books and then shows that each copy still needed handwork.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text qualifies how complete the change was in the 1450s; it does not dismiss the press's importance.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says buyers chose decoration they "could afford" but never describes particular styles.
